title: tool-package
description: The parsed content of one tools/packages/<id>.toml: a set of tools an operator enables together from the administration page's Tools section (D101). A tool no package names is built in and always present. A package is part of the release — its tools' manifests and programs ship with the server and the client like every other tool's — so enabling one downloads nothing and never hands a client code it does not already hold (D3). What it may need on the user's machine is a program the user installs themselves (`requires`), and a long-running companion the client starts when a tool needs it (`host`).

id.description: Must equal the file's name without `.toml`. The name the baseline's `packages` lists.

summary.description: One line under the heading, for a person deciding whether to enable it.

description.description: What the package lets someone do, what it needs, and what enabling it exposes — written for the operator, not the model. Each tool's own `description` is what the model is told.

publisher.description: Who wrote it. Both are reviewed into the release; `community` says the tools came from outside the project and the project maintains them less closely.

tools.description: The tool names this package holds. Each must have a manifest, and a tool belongs to at most one package.

requires.description: A program the user installs on their own machine for the tools to work. Neuman never downloads it: when it is missing, a dispatch is refused with `missing_program` and a sentence naming it and where to get it, which the model passes on.

program.description: The executable's name, looked for on the PATH the Neuman client runs with.

host.description: A long-running companion — a program in a window the user works in — that the package's tools talk to over a `0600` Unix socket in the user's runtime directory. The client starts it when one of the tools is dispatched and nothing answers, and leaves it running: closing its window ends it, and the next call starts it again.

exec.description: Resolved from the client's own trusted tool directory, exactly as a manifest's `exec` is (D3) — never a path. No manifest names it, so no dispatch can run it.
